notes.variety: Zürich German (Züritüütsch) as people actually type it in messages and speak it in the city: no fixed orthography, so this file uses one consistent informal spelling (nöd, cha, wott, gsi, isch). Zürich is chosen because it is the variety a learner hears most and because most Swiss will understand it. Bernese (Bärndütsch) and Basel differences are noted only where they are large. The learner also studies Standard German, so notes flag every place the dialect diverges from it.
notes.turns: Swiss German has no Präteritum at all: every past is the Perfekt (ich bin ggange, ich ha gschaffet), including for sii and haa (ich bin gsi, ich ha gha), and there is no past perfect except a doubled Perfekt (ich ha gha gschaffet) that speech rarely needs. There is no progressive form; the present covers habits and right now, and 'am' plus infinitive (ich bin am schaffe) adds the mid-action sense when it matters. The future is the present plus a time word (ich gang morn), with 'wird' reserved for guesses and promises. Conditionals use 'würd' plus infinitive or the short forms wär, hett, chönnt, müesst, wett, and the third conditional is 'hett' plus participle (ich hett das gmacht). Subjunctive I for reported speech does not exist: you report with 'er hät gseit, dass' or with 'er heigi / er sägi', the dialect's own reportive forms. Passive exists (es wird gmacht, es isch gmacht worde) but the dialect prefers 'me' (one) as subject.
notes.wordOrder: Verb-second in main clauses and verb-final in subordinate clauses, exactly as in Standard German: 'wil' and 'dass' send the conjugated verb to the end (Ich chume nöd, wil ich mues schaffe). The big dialect difference is the double 'go' before infinitives of motion: ich gang go poschte, chunsch cho ässe. Modal plus infinitive keeps the infinitive at the end (ich wott hüt öppis chaufe), and in subordinate clauses the modal usually comes before the infinitive rather than after (wil ich mues schaffe, not wil ich schaffe mues). Questions invert or just rise (Chunsch mit?). Every relative clause is introduced by 'wo', whatever the antecedent or role.
notes.slotGrammar: Three genders with articles de / d / s (de Maa, d Frau, s Chind) and plural d (d Lüüt); indefinite en / e / es. Only two spoken cases matter: nominative-accusative (identical) and dative (em / de / em, en with a preposition: mit em Zug, bi de Frau). There is no genitive at all: possession is 'vo' (s Auto vo mim Brüeder) or the dative construction (mim Brüeder sis Auto). Adjectives take endings only before a noun (en guete Wii, es guets Bier) and stay bare after sii (de Wii isch guet). Pronouns: ich, du, er/sie/es, mir, ir, si; object mich/dich/ihn, mir/dir/ihm.
notes.sound: The ch is a harsh throat scrape (ach-sound) everywhere, even at the start of a word: Chind, chaufe, cha; there is no soft ich-sound. k in most words has become kch or ch (Kafi, dänke), and English speakers must drop the puff of air after k, p, t. Vowels can be long or short and change meaning (Wääg way, Wäg weigh), and the open ä is much more frequent than in Standard German (gäll, Wätter). Standard German ei and au have split: 'Ziit' (Zeit) keeps the old ii, 'Huus' (Haus) keeps the old uu. Stress is on the first syllable even in loanwords (BAlkon, BÜro), and the ending -e is a full, clear vowel, never swallowed.
notes.register: Sie and du both exist: du with Hoi / Sali for friends, colleagues, anyone under about forty and most shop staff in a casual setting; Sie with Grüezi for strangers, officials, older people and formal service. The chunk changes with the pronoun: Chasch mer hälfe? becomes Chönd Si mer hälfe?, Hoi becomes Grüezi, and Tschüss / Ciao becomes Uf Widerluege / Adieu. Swiss switch to du faster than Germans and use first names in offices, but never open a formal email in dialect.

turnGrid.note: Perfekt only: the dialect has no Präteritum, so 'ich ging' does not exist. sii/haa too: ich bin gsi, ich ha gha.

turnGrid.form: ich bin grad am Gaa gsi
turnGrid.gloss: I was (in the middle of) going
turnGrid.note: No imperfect. Background is 'am + infinitive' inside the Perfekt, or just the Perfekt plus 'grad' (just then).
Doubled Perfekt (Perfekt II): participle plus gsi/gha. Speech mostly uses plain Perfekt with 'scho' or 'vorhär' instead.
One form for habit and now. gaa is irregular: gang, gasch, gaat, gönd, gönd, gönd. Standard 'ich gehe'.
'am + infinitive' is the only progressive and is far more common than in Standard German (ich bin am Ässe). Otherwise use the present.
Same form as the past simple cell: the Perfekt is both 'I went' and 'I have gone'. 'Have been going since' is present plus sit (ich gang sit zwei Jahr).

turnGrid.gloss: I will go / I am going to go
turnGrid.note: Present plus a time word is the normal future. 'wird + infinitive' is for guesses (er wird scho cho) and promises, and is rarer than in Standard German.
No such tense. Present 'am + infinitive' plus a time word (dänn, am Achti) does the job.
No future perfect. Perfekt plus 'dänn scho' (by then already), or 'bis dänn bin ich ggange'. 'ich wird ggange sii' sounds bookish.

items.target: Hoi, wie gaats? / Grüezi, wie gaats Ine?
items.gloss: Hi, how's it going? / Hello, how are you (formal)?

example.target: Hoi Arjun, wie gaats? — Guet, und dir? — Au guet. Tschau, bis spöter!
example.gloss: Hi Arjun, how's it going? — Good, and you? — Also good. Bye, see you later!

items.note: Uses C-HELLO-BYE. Grüezi is the Zürich Sie-greeting (Bern: Grüessech); Hoi and Sali go with du. Goodbye: Tschau/Tschüss (du), Uf Widerluege/Adieu (Sie).

items.target: Ich bi de/d ___, ich chume us ___ / ich schaffe als ___
items.gloss: I'm ___, I come from ___ / I work as ___

example.target: Ich bi de Arjun, ich chume us Indie und ich schaffe als Ingenieur.
example.gloss: I'm Arjun, I come from India and I work as an engineer.

items.note: Recipe: C-MY-NAME, D-BE, G-AND, G-FROM. Names take an article in dialect: ich bi de Arjun, das isch d Anna. Standard German 'Ich heiße' is dialect 'ich heisse', but 'ich bi de' is more common.

items.target: Merci vilmal! — Bitte / Gärn gscheh
items.gloss: Thanks a lot! — You're welcome / Gladly done

example.target: Merci vilmal für d Hilf. — Gärn gscheh, kes Problem.
example.gloss: Thanks a lot for the help. — You're welcome, no problem.

items.note: Uses C-PLEASE-THANKS. Merci (stress on MER) is the everyday thanks; Danke is a bit more formal. 'Gärn gscheh' is the warm reply Germans don't use.

items.target: Was choscht das? / Wie vil choscht das?
items.gloss: What does that cost? / How much does that cost?

example.target: Was choscht de Kafi? — Vier füfzg. — Und s Gipfeli? — Eis zwänzg.
example.gloss: What does the coffee cost? — Four fifty. — And the croissant? — One twenty.

items.note: Uses C-HOW-MUCH, T-WH. Prices are read as 'vier füfzg', never with Franke and Rappe spelled out. 'Wie tüür isch das?' also works.

items.target: Excusé, wo isch ___? / Isch das wiit?
items.gloss: Excuse me, where is ___? / Is that far?

example.target: Excusé, wo isch de Bahnhof? — Graduus, dänn links. — Isch das wiit? — Nei, füf Minute.
example.gloss: Excuse me, where's the station? — Straight on, then left. — Is it far? — No, five minutes.

items.note: Uses C-SORRY, C-WHERE-IS, T-WH. Listen for: graduus (straight), links, rächts, näbet (next to), gägenüber (opposite), hinde (behind). 'Wiit' is Standard 'weit'.

items.target: Sorry, ich verstaa das nöd. Chönd Si das langsamer säge?
items.gloss: Sorry, I don't understand. Could you say that more slowly?

example.target: Sorry, ich ha das nöd verstande. Chasch das nomal säge, bitte langsam?
example.gloss: Sorry, I didn't understand that. Can you say that again, slowly please?

items.note: Uses C-SORRY, C-DONT-UNDERSTAND, C-REPEAT-PLEASE. Say 'ich ha nöd verstande' (Perfekt) for what was just said; many Swiss will switch to Standard German, so add 'Dialäkt isch okay'.

items.target: Ich ha ___ gern / Ich mag ___ nöd

example.target: Ich ha Chäs gern, aber Fisch mag ich gar nöd.
example.gloss: I like cheese, but I don't like fish at all.

items.note: Uses D-LIKE, T-NEG. 'gern haa' and 'möge' both take the plain noun (accusative = nominative); 'mir gfallt' is for things you see or hear (music, a flat).

items.target: Ich hett gern ___ / Ich nimm ___

example.target: Ich hett gern es Kafi und es Gipfeli, bitte. — Gärn. Süscht no öppis? — Nei, merci.
example.gloss: I'd like a coffee and a croissant, please. — Sure. Anything else? — No, thanks.

items.note: Uses D-WOULD-LIKE, G-AND. Ordering is 'ich hett gern' or 'ich nimm'; 'ich wott' is blunt and 'ich möchte' is Standard German. Note 'es Kafi' (neuter), not 'einen Kaffee'.

items.target: ich bi ___

example.target: Ich bi müed, aber ich bi zfride.
example.gloss: I'm tired, but I'm content.

items.note: sii: bi, bisch, isch, sind, sind, sind. No Präteritum: 'was' is 'ich bi gsi'. Adjective after sii takes no ending.

items.target: ich ha ___

example.target: Ich ha zwei Chind und ich ha immer Hunger.
example.gloss: I have two kids and I'm always hungry.

items.note: haa: ha, häsch, hät, händ, händ, händ. Also hunger and thirst (ich ha Hunger/Durscht), but age is sii: ich bi drissg. 'had' is 'ich ha gha'.

items.target: es hät ___

example.target: Es hät e Beiz um d Egge, und es hät au en Coop.
example.gloss: There's a pub around the corner, and there's also a Coop.

items.note: Dialect uses 'es hät' for both singular and plural, not Standard 'es gibt' (which sounds German). Negation: es hät kei Bänk / es hät niemert.

items.target: ich ha ___ gern / ich mag ___

example.target: Ich ha Bier gern, aber Wii mag ich nöd so.
example.gloss: I like beer, but I don't like wine so much.

items.note: 'gern' goes to the end after the noun. For activities use the verb plus gern: ich gang gern go wandere. Not 'ich gern haa' order.

items.target: ich wott ___ / ich wott ___ (V)

example.target: Ich wott hüt am Abig i d Stadt gaa.
example.gloss: I want to go into town this evening.

items.note: wele: wott, wotsch, wott, wänd, wänd, wänd. Standard 'ich will' is dialect 'ich wott'; blunt like English 'I want', so order with D-WOULD-LIKE. Infinitive goes to the end.

items.target: ich hett gern ___ / ich wett gern ___ (V)

example.target: Ich hett gern es Bier. Und ich wett gern zahle.
example.gloss: I'd like a beer. And I'd like to pay.

items.note: 'hett gern' + noun for ordering, 'wett gern' + verb for wishes. 'möchte' is understood but marks you as speaking Standard German.

items.target: ich bruuche ___ / ich mues ___ (V)

example.target: Ich bruuche e neui Jacke, und ich mues no go poschte.
example.gloss: I need a new jacket, and I still need to go shopping.

items.note: bruuche takes a plain noun (Standard 'brauchen'). 'need to' is simply 'mues' plus infinitive; 'bruuche z' exists but is rarer than in German.

items.target: ich cha ___

example.target: Ich cha guet choche, aber ich cha nöd singe.
example.gloss: I can cook well, but I can't sing.

items.note: chöne: cha, chasch, cha, chönd, chönd, chönd. Infinitive at the end, negation 'nöd' before it. Ability and permission both, like Standard 'kann'.

items.target: ich gang go ___ / ich wird ___

example.target: Ich gang morn go schwümme. Und du?
example.gloss: I'm going swimming tomorrow. And you?

items.note: 'go' is a dialect particle before infinitives of motion (gang go ässe, chum cho luege), obligatory and absent from Standard German. Intention otherwise is the present plus a time word.

items.target: ich wird ___ / ich ___ (dänn)

example.target: Ich wird dir dänn schriibe, wänn ich daa bi.
example.gloss: I'll write to you when I'm there.

items.note: wärde: wird, wirsch, wird, wärded. 'wird' marks a promise or guess; for plans use the present: ich chume morn (I'll come tomorrow).

items.target: stem + -e, -sch, -t, -ed, -ed, -ed

example.target: Ich schaffe i Züri und ich wohne z Winterthur.
example.gloss: I work in Zürich and I live in Winterthur.

items.note: One plural ending for all three persons (mir/ir/si schaffed), unlike Standard German. The present also covers the future with a time word.

items.target: ich bi am + infinitive

example.target: Ich bi grad am Choche, ich lüüte spöter aa.
example.gloss: I'm cooking right now, I'll call later.

items.note: 'am + infinitive' is used far more than Standard 'beim ...' and is the normal way to say 'right now'. Without 'am' the present is fine too.

items.target: ich bi/ha + participle (gsi, ggange, gha, gmacht)

example.target: Geschter bin ich z Bärn gsi und ha en Fründ gseh.
example.gloss: Yesterday I was in Bern and saw a friend.

items.note: No Präteritum: 'war', 'ging', 'hatte' do not exist. Learn the four participles first: gsi (been), ggange (gone), gha (had), gmacht (done).

items.target: present + time word / wird + infinitive

example.target: Am Samschtig gang ich uf Luzern. Es wird sicher schön.
example.gloss: On Saturday I'm going to Lucerne. It'll surely be nice.

items.note: The present with morn, am Samschtig, nächschti Wuche is the default. 'wird' is for guesses and weather, less for plans.

items.target: nöd (verb) / kei + noun

example.target: Ich chume nöd. Ich ha kei Ziit und kei Luscht.
example.gloss: I'm not coming. I have no time and no desire.

items.note: 'nöd' is Standard 'nicht' and goes where nicht goes (after the object, before infinitive). 'kei' replaces ein/kein before nouns; Bern says 'nid', Basel 'nit'.

items.target: verb + subject ... ? / statement + rising tone

example.target: Chunsch hüt mit? — Ja, gern. Häsch Ziit?
example.gloss: Are you coming along today? — Yes, gladly. Do you have time?

items.note: Invert verb and du, then drop 'du' entirely: chunsch, häsch, bisch (the -sch ending carries the subject). Add 'oder?' at the end for 'right?'.

items.target: wär, was, wo, wänn, wie, wie vil, warum

example.target: Wo wohnsch? Wänn chunsch? Wie vil choscht das?
example.gloss: Where do you live? When are you coming? How much does that cost?

items.note: Question word, then verb, then subject (if any). 'wo' is where, 'wänn' is when, 'wär' is who. Warum and wieso are interchangeable.

example.target: Ich nimm es Bier und en Salat.
example.gloss: I'll take a beer and a salad.

items.note: No word-order change. Often shortened to 'u' in Bernese; Zürich keeps 'und'.

example.target: Ich chäm gern, aber ich mues schaffe.
example.gloss: I'd love to come, but I have to work.

items.note: Coordinator: verb stays second after 'aber'. 'sondern' after a negative exists but speech mostly uses 'aber' too.

items.target: ___ oder ___

example.target: Wotsch Tee oder Kafi?
example.gloss: Do you want tea or coffee?

items.note: No word-order change. Tag 'oder?' at the end of a sentence means 'right?', a real Swiss tic.

items.target: ___, wil ___ (verb at end)

example.target: Ich cha nöd cho, wil ich mues schaffe.
example.gloss: I can't come, because I have to work.

items.note: 'wil' (Standard 'weil') sends the verb to the end, but dialect puts the modal before the infinitive: 'wil ich mues schaffe', not 'schaffe mues'. 'will' is a different word.

items.target: dänn / nachhär

example.target: Zerscht gang ich go poschte, dänn choche ich.
example.gloss: First I go shopping, then I cook.

items.note: Time adverb in first position pushes the subject after the verb: 'dänn choche ich'. 'dänn' is also 'in that case'.

items.target: au

example.target: Ich chume au. Er hät au kei Ziit.
example.gloss: I'm coming too. He also has no time.

items.note: 'au' (Standard 'auch') sits after the verb or the pronoun. 'Ich au' = me too, 'ich au nöd' = me neither.

items.target: i / im / i de (place), im (month)

example.target: Ich wohne i Züri, im Zäntrum. Im Mai isch es schön.
example.gloss: I live in Zürich, in the centre. In May it's nice.

items.note: 'i' becomes 'im' with neuter/masculine dative and 'i de' with feminine: im Büro, i de Stadt. Before a town name 'z' (z Bärn) is also common.

items.target: uf / am (day)

example.target: Am Samschtig gaan ich uf Bärn. S Buech liit uf em Tisch.
example.gloss: On Saturday I'm going to Bern. The book is lying on the table.

items.note: Days take 'am' (am Mäntig). 'uf' means on top of and also 'to' for towns and mountains (uf Bärn). Dative after position: uf em Tisch.

items.target: am (time) / bi (person, place)

example.target: Mir träffed üs am Sächsi bim Bahnhof.
example.gloss: We'll meet at six at the station.

items.note: Clock times take 'am' plus -i (am Sächsi = at six). 'bi' is at someone's or by a landmark: bi mir, bim Coop. Standard 'um sechs' is not used.

items.target: vo / us (origin)

example.target: Ich chume us Indie. Das isch vo mim Brüeder.
example.gloss: I come from India. That's from my brother.

items.note: 'us' for coming out of a country or town, 'vo' for people, things and 'from ... to'. Both take the dative: vo de Anna, us em Büro.

items.target: uf / nach / zu / i (direction)

example.target: Ich gang uf Bärn, dänn zum Zahnarzt, und morn i d Stadt.
example.gloss: I'm going to Bern, then to the dentist, and tomorrow into town.

items.note: Towns take 'uf' (uf Züri) in the east and 'nach' in the west; people take 'zu' (zum Arzt); 'i' plus accusative for going into (i d Stadt).

items.target: mit ___ (dative)

example.target: Ich gang mit em Zug und mit mine Fründe.
example.gloss: I'm going by train and with my friends.

items.note: Always dative: mit em, mit de, mit mine (plural). Vehicles use 'mit' too: mit em Velo, mit em Bus.

items.target: ich, du, er/si/es, mir, ir, si / Si

example.target: Mir gönd hei, ir bliibed daa. Chömed Si au?
example.gloss: We're going home, you (pl.) stay here. Are you (formal) coming too?

items.note: 'mir' is 'we' (Standard 'wir'), a classic trap. 'du' vanishes in questions (chunsch?). Sie is 'Si', spoken Sii, with verb -ed.

items.target: mich, dich, ihn, si, es, üs, eu, si / mir, dir, ihm, ire, üs, eu, ine

example.target: Ich gseh dich morn. Chasch mer hälfe? Gib ihm s Buech.
example.gloss: I'll see you tomorrow. Can you help me? Give him the book.

items.note: Unstressed forms shrink: 'mer' (mir), 'der' (dir), 'em' (ihm), 'ere' (ihr). Standard 'euch' is 'eu' and 'uns' is 'üs'.

items.target: de, d, s (the) / en, e, es (a)

example.target: De Maa, d Frau und s Chind sind i de Stadt. Es Kafi, bitte.
example.gloss: The man, the woman and the child are in town. A coffee, please.

items.note: 'd' and 's' are single consonants glued to the noun (d Frau, s Huus). Dative: em, de, em / eme, ere, eme. Names take an article: de Peter, d Anna.

items.target: masculine de, feminine d, neuter s; adjective -e, -i, -s

example.target: En guete Wii, e gueti Suppe, es guets Bier.
example.gloss: A good wine, a good soup, a good beer.

items.note: Same three genders as Standard German, mostly the same words, but note s Tram, de Butter, s Kafi (neuter), s Foto. Adjectives agree before a noun only.

items.target: d + noun; -e, -er, umlaut or no change

example.target: Ei Chind, zwei Chind; ei Huus, zwei Hüüser; ei Frau, zwei Fraue.
example.gloss: One child, two children; one house, two houses; one woman, two women.

items.note: Standard -n plurals often lose the -n (Fraue, Strasse); the article d marks plural for all genders. Dative plural adds -e: mit de Chinde.

items.target: dä / die / das (this, that) ; die (these, those)

example.target: Dä Maa, die Frau, das Chind. Die Schue sind tüür.
example.gloss: That man, that woman, that child. Those shoes are expensive.

items.note: 'dä' is masculine (Standard 'der/dieser'), 'die' feminine and plural, 'das' neuter. Pointing: dä daa (this one here), dä dete (that one there).

items.target: eis, zwei, drü, vier, föif, sächs, sibe, acht, nüün, zää; erschti

example.target: Es choscht zwöiezwänzg füfzg. Ich wohne im dritte Stock.
example.gloss: It costs twenty-two fifty. I live on the third floor.

items.note: 'eis/ei/en' by gender, 'drü' is three, 'föif/füf' five, 'zää' ten, 'zwänzg' twenty. Units before tens as in German: föifezwänzg.

items.target: de Name (name), d Adrässe (address), s Alter (age), de Beruef (job), d Studäntin (student f.), de Studänt (student m.), de Schwiizer (Swiss man), d Schwiizerin (Swiss woman), Indie (India), indisch (Indian), Amerika (USA), ledig (single), verhüratet (married), d Sprach (language), s Handy (phone), d E-Mail (email)
items.note: Use D-BE: ich bi drissg, ich bi ledig, ich bi Ingenieur. No article before jobs and nationalities.

items.target: d Muetter (mother), de Vatter (father), d Eltere (parents), de Brüeder (brother), d Schwöschter (sister), s Chind (child), d Chind (children), de Sohn (son), d Tochter (daughter), d Frau (wife), de Maa (husband), d Grosi (grandma), de Grosspapi (grandpa), de Fründ (friend/boyfriend), d Fründin (friend/girlfriend), d Lüüt (people)
items.note: 'Fründ' is both friend and boyfriend; say 'en Kolleg' for a friend who is not a partner. 'd Lüüt' is 'people' (Standard 'Leute').

items.target: s Kafi (coffee), s Brot (bread), s Gipfeli (croissant), de Chäs (cheese), d Wurscht (sausage), s Fleisch (meat), s Gmües (vegetables), d Rüebli (carrots), d Härdöpfel (potatoes), s Bier (beer), de Wii (wine), s Wasser (water), d Milch (milk), d Beiz (pub), znüni (mid-morning snack), zmittag (lunch)
items.note: Meals are verbs: zmörgele, zmittage, znachte. 'es Stange' is a small draft beer, 'es Kafi crème' the default coffee. 'Rüebli' and 'Härdöpfel' are pure dialect.

items.target: hüt (today), morn (tomorrow), geschter (yesterday), jetzt (now), spöter (later), d Wuche (week), de Mäntig (Monday), de Ziischtig (Tuesday), de Mittwuch (Wednesday), de Donschtig (Thursday), de Friitig (Friday), de Samschtig (Saturday), de Sunntig (Sunday), am Morge (in the morning), am Abig (in the evening), am Sächsi (at six), halbi sibni (half past six), Viertel ab (quarter past)
items.note: 'morn' is tomorrow and 'am Morge' is in the morning: keep them apart. Clock: 'halbi sibni' = 6:30, 'Viertel vor achti' = 7:45, 'zää ab sibni' = 7:10.

items.target: de Bahnhof (station), d Halteschtell (stop), s Tram (tram), de Bus (bus), d Poscht (post office), d Bank (bank), d Apitheek (pharmacy), s Spital (hospital), d Chile (church), de See (lake), d Strass (street), de Platz (square), links (left), rächts (right), graduus (straight on), näbet (next to)
items.note: 's Tram' is neuter in Swiss German (Standard 'die Tram'). 'Apitheek' and 'Spital' differ from Apotheke and Krankenhaus.

items.target: gaa (go), cho (come), ässe (eat), trinke (drink), gseh (see), mache (do/make), säge (say), wüsse (know), gää (give), nää (take), wohne (live), schaffe (work), chaufe (buy), rede (speak), läse (read), schriibe (write), schlaafe (sleep), spile (play), lerne (learn), wele (want), gern haa (like), bruuche (need), haa (have), sii (be), luege (look)
items.note: Short infinitives: gaa, cho, gää, nää, sii, haa (Standard gehen, kommen, geben, nehmen, sein, haben). 'schaffe' is work, not create; 'luege' is look.

items.target: Ch (throat) everywhere, kch, long ii/uu/üü, open ä, full final -e
items.gloss: Sounds that do not exist in English
items.note: Every ch is the harsh ach-sound, even in Chind, Chuchichäschtli (kitchen cupboard, the famous test word). Standard k is often kch (Kafi = kchafi). Long vowels are written doubled: Ziit, Huus, Müüs.

items.target: First-syllable stress, also in loanwords; no reduced schwa
items.note: Stress the first syllable even where German or French stresses later: BÜro, BAlkon, MERci, KAfi. Final -e is a clear short e (schaffe = SCHAF-fe), never swallowed.

items.target: Hoi / Sali — Tschau / Grüezi — Uf Widerluege

example.target: Hoi zäme! ... Also, tschau, bis morn!
example.gloss: Hi everyone! ... Right, bye, see you tomorrow!

items.note: 'Hoi zäme' greets a group. Grüezi (Zürich) / Grüessech (Bern) is the formal hello; 'Adieu' (ade) is a formal goodbye, not French-sounding to Swiss ears.

items.target: bitte / merci (vilmal) / gärn gscheh

example.target: Es Kafi, bitte. — Gärn. — Merci vilmal! — Gärn gscheh.
example.gloss: A coffee, please. — Sure. — Thanks a lot! — You're welcome.

items.note: 'Merci' is the neutral thanks (stress MER-ci), 'Danke' is slightly more formal. Waiters answer 'gärn' to an order.

items.target: Sorry / Excusé / Es tuet mer leid

example.target: Excusé, dörf ich schnell verbii? — Sorry, ich ha dich nöd gseh.
example.gloss: Excuse me, may I get past? — Sorry, I didn't see you.

items.note: 'Excusé' (from French) is for getting attention or past someone; 'Sorry' is the everyday apology; 'Es tuet mer leid' is for real regret.

items.target: Was choscht das? / Wie vil macht das?
items.gloss: How much is it? / How much does that come to?

example.target: Was choscht das? — Zwölf Franke.
example.gloss: How much is this? — Twelve francs.

items.note: 'macht' is for the total at the till. 'Franke' is plural too; 'Stutz' is slang for francs.

items.target: Wo isch ___?

example.target: Wo isch s WC? — Hinde links.
example.gloss: Where is the toilet? — At the back on the left.

items.note: 'Wo' plus 'isch' plus the noun with its article. Plural: 'Wo sind d Toilette?'. Not 'wo isch de WC' (WC is neuter: s WC).

items.target: Ich verstaa nöd / Ich ha nöd verstande
items.gloss: I don't understand / I didn't understand

example.target: Sorry, ich ha das nöd verstande.
example.gloss: Sorry, I didn't understand that.

items.note: Perfekt 'ich ha nöd verstande' for what was just said. 'Ich verstaa nöd' is for the general state (I don't get it).

items.target: Chasch das nomal säge? / Chönd Si das langsamer säge?
items.gloss: Can you say that again? / Could you say that more slowly?

example.target: Chönd Si das bitte nomal säge, e chli langsamer?
example.gloss: Could you please say that again, a bit more slowly?

items.note: 'nomal' (Standard 'noch einmal') is the word for again. 'e chli' (a bit) softens any request. Dialect 'cha' is used for polite could too.

items.target: Ich bi de/d ___ / Freut mi

example.target: Hoi, ich bi de Arjun. — Sali, ich bi d Lea. Freut mi!
example.gloss: Hi, I'm Arjun. — Hi, I'm Lea. Nice to meet you!

items.note: Article before first names: de for men, d for women. 'Freut mi' is the reply; 'angenehm' is old-fashioned.

items.target: Häsch Luscht, ___ z ___? / Chunsch mit go ___?
items.gloss: Do you feel like ___? / Are you coming along to ___?

example.target: Häsch Luscht, am Friitig go ässe z gaa? — Ja, gern!
example.gloss: Do you feel like going out to eat on Friday? — Yes, gladly!

items.note: Uses C-WOULD-YOU-LIKE, D-LETS, T-Q. 'Häsch Luscht' (do you have desire) is the standard invitation; 'Chunsch mit?' the shortest. Note 'go ässe' before an infinitive of motion.

items.target: Ja, gern! / Merci, aber ich cha leider nöd, wil ___
items.gloss: Yes, gladly! / Thanks, but unfortunately I can't, because ___

example.target: Das isch lieb, aber am Friitig gaats nöd, wil ich mues lang schaffe.
example.gloss: That's kind, but Friday doesn't work, because I have to work late.

items.note: Recipe: C-THANKS-BUT, D-CAN, G-BECAUSE, D-HAVE-TO. 'Es gaat nöd' (it doesn't work) is the softest refusal. In the wil-clause the modal precedes the infinitive.

items.target: Wie wärs mit ___? / Sölled mer ___?

example.target: Wie wärs mit Donschtig am Sibni bim Bahnhof? Passt das?
example.gloss: How about Thursday at seven at the station? Does that work?

items.note: Uses C-HOW-ABOUT, D-LETS, G-AT. 'Passt das?' or 'Gaat das?' is the natural check. 'wärs' = wär es, the conditional of sii.

items.target: Sorry, ich bi z spaat, ich ha ___ / Es tuet mer leid
items.gloss: Sorry, I'm late, I ___ / I'm sorry

example.target: Sorry, dass ich z spaat bi, s Tram isch nöd cho.
example.gloss: Sorry that I'm late, the tram didn't come.

items.note: Uses C-SORRY-LATE, G-BECAUSE, T-PAST. Explain in the Perfekt; 'es tuet mer leid' for genuine apology, 'sorry' for small things.

items.target: Ich hett gern ___ / Was isch ___? / Zahle, bitte
items.gloss: I'd like ___ / What is ___? / The bill, please

example.target: Was isch es Cordon bleu? — Schnitzel mit Chäs und Schinke. — Guet, das nimm ich.
example.gloss: What's a cordon bleu? — Schnitzel with cheese and ham. — Good, I'll take that.

items.note: Uses D-WOULD-LIKE, C-WHAT-MEAN, C-BILL. 'Ich nimm' (I'll take) is the ordering verb; 'Zahle, bitte' or 'Chönd mer zahle?' gets the bill. Tip is rounded up, not 15%.

items.target: Was heisst ___? / Wie schriibt me das?
items.gloss: What does ___ mean? / How do you spell that?

example.target: Was heisst 'Chuchichäschtli'? — Küchenschrank. — Wie schriibt me das?
example.gloss: What does 'Chuchichäschtli' mean? — Kitchen cupboard. — How do you spell that?

items.note: Uses C-WHAT-MEAN, T-WH. 'Was heisst X uf Hochdütsch?' is the killer question: Swiss will happily translate dialect into Standard German for you.

items.target: Zerscht ha ich ___, dänn bin ich ___

example.target: Am Samschtig bin ich zerscht go poschte, und dänn ha ich mit Fründe gässe.
example.gloss: On Saturday I first went shopping, and then I ate with friends.

items.note: Recipe: G-SEQUENCE, D-HAVE-DONE, G-BEFORE-AFTER. Everything in the Perfekt, participle at the end. 'go poschte' after 'bin' because it is a motion.

items.target: Wänn träffed mer üs? / Am ___ bim ___, gaat das?
items.gloss: When shall we meet? / At ___ at the ___, does that work?

example.target: Wänn träffed mer üs? — Am Sächsi bim Bahnhof? — Guet, bis dänn!
example.gloss: When shall we meet? — At six at the station? — Good, see you then!

items.note: Uses C-HOW-ABOUT, G-AT, C-SEE-YOU. 'sich träffe' is reflexive: mir träffed üs. Confirm with 'abgmacht' (agreed) or 'passt'.

items.target: ich mues ___

example.target: Ich mues morn früeh uufstaa.
example.gloss: I have to get up early tomorrow.

items.note: müese: mues, muesch, mues, müend, müend, müend. Covers both 'have to' and 'must'. Infinitive at the end, but after wil: 'wil ich mues uufstaa'.

items.target: ich mues ___ / du muesch nöd ___ / du dörfsch nöd ___
items.gloss: I must ___ / you needn't ___ / you mustn't ___

example.target: Du muesch nöd cho, aber du dörfsch nöd z spaat sii.
example.gloss: You needn't come, but you mustn't be late.

items.note: Same trap as Standard German: 'muesch nöd' means no need, not prohibition. Prohibition is 'dörfsch nöd' (dörfe = dürfen).

items.target: ich sött ___ / du söttsch ___

example.target: Du söttsch meh schlaafe, und ich sött weniger schaffe.
example.gloss: You should sleep more, and I should work less.

items.note: sölle: sött, söttsch, sött, sötted. 'sött' is already the conditional (Standard 'sollte'); the plain 'soll' is used for reported orders. Advice always uses 'sött'.

items.target: Chöntsch ___? / Chönd Si ___? / ich ha ___ chöne

example.target: Chöntsch mer schnell hälfe? Geschter ha ich nöd cho chöne.
example.gloss: Could you help me quickly? Yesterday I couldn't come.

items.note: 'chöntsch' (Standard 'könntest') is the polite request. Past of chöne is Perfekt with a bare infinitive instead of a participle: ha ... chöne.

items.target: villicht ___ / es chönnt sii, dass ___

example.target: Villicht rägnets morn. Es chönnt sii, dass er spöter chunt.
example.gloss: Maybe it'll rain tomorrow. It could be that he comes later.

items.note: 'villicht' plus present is the everyday 'might'. 'es chönnt sii, dass' is the verb version; 'mag' does not mean might in dialect.

items.target: früener ha ich ___ (Perfekt) / früener bin ich immer ___

example.target: Früener ha ich jede Tag Fuessball gspilt.
example.gloss: I used to play football every day.

items.note: No imperfect, so 'used to' is 'früener' (earlier) plus the Perfekt, optionally with 'immer' or 'meischtens'. Standard 'spielte' has no dialect form.

items.target: ich ha scho ___ / ich bi no nie ___
items.gloss: I have already ___ / I have never ___

example.target: Ich bi scho z Rom gsi, aber ich ha no nie Pizza gmacht.
example.gloss: I've already been to Rome, but I've never made pizza.

items.note: Experience uses the same Perfekt as yesterday's events: 'scho' (already), 'no nie' (never yet), 'scho mal' (ever) carry the meaning.

items.target: ich bi grad am ___ gsi, wo ___

example.target: Ich bi grad am Ässe gsi, wo du aaglüütet häsch.
example.gloss: I was just eating when you called.

items.note: 'am + infinitive' inside the Perfekt (bi ... gsi). 'wo' means 'when' for the past (Standard 'als'); 'wänn' is only for present, future and repeated events.

items.target: ich hoffe/versueche/vergisse, ___ z ___

example.target: Ich versueche, morn früener z cho. Ich hoffe, s chlappt.
example.gloss: I'm trying to come earlier tomorrow. I hope it works out.

items.note: 'z' before the infinitive (Standard 'zu'), infinitive at the end. Plan and decide are usually 'ich wott' or 'ich ha beschlosse, dass'. 'ha vergässe z' for forgot to.

items.target: ich ___ gern / ich ha nüt dagäge, ___ z ___

example.target: Ich choche gern. Ich ha nüt dagäge, spaat z ässe.
example.gloss: I enjoy cooking. I don't mind eating late.

items.note: No -ing: 'enjoy doing' is verb plus 'gern'; 'keep doing' is 'immer wieder' plus verb; 'finish doing' is 'fertig' plus verb (ich bi fertig gschaffet).

items.target: ich dänke, (dass) ___ / ich weiss, dass ___

example.target: Ich dänke, er chunt spöter. Ich weiss, dass er kei Ziit hät.
example.gloss: I think he's coming later. I know that he has no time.

items.note: With 'dass' the verb goes to the end (hät); without 'dass' the clause keeps main-clause order. 'Ich glaub' is the most common opener.

items.target: Sölled mer ___? / Chum, mir ___

example.target: Sölled mer go ässe? — Ja, chum, mir gönd i d Beiz.
example.gloss: Shall we go eat? — Yes, come on, let's go to the pub.

items.note: 'Sölled mer' (Standard 'sollen wir') is the question form; 'chum' plus mir plus verb is the imperative version. No 'lass uns' in dialect.

items.target: bi/ha + am + infinitive + gsi

example.target: Ich bi am Schlaafe gsi, wo s Telefon glüütet hät.
example.gloss: I was sleeping when the phone rang.

items.note: There is no imperfect: the background action is Perfekt plus 'am'. For habits and states use plain Perfekt with 'früener' or 'immer'.

items.target: ha/bi + Partizip (g- prefix)

example.target: Ich ha hüt scho drü Kafi trunke.
example.gloss: I've already drunk three coffees today.

items.note: This is THE past tense: it means 'I did' and 'I have done'. Participles keep 'g-' without a vowel: gmacht, gseh, gsi, trunke (no g- after t/d).

items.target: Wänn ___ (verb-final), dänn ___ (present)

example.target: Wänn s morn rägnet, bliib ich dihei.
example.gloss: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay at home.

items.note: 'wänn' = both if and when; verb at the end of the wänn-clause, then verb first in the main clause. Both halves in the present, never 'wird'.

items.target: present + time word

example.target: Ich triff si morn am Zwölfi zum Zmittag.
example.gloss: I'm meeting her tomorrow at twelve for lunch.

items.note: The present is the default future: 'ich gang', 'ich chume', 'mir träffed üs'. Adding 'wird' would make it sound like a guess.

items.target: stem! / -ed! (plural) / -ed Si! (formal)

example.target: Chum! Lueg! — Chömed ine! — Nämed Si Platz!
example.gloss: Come! Look! — Come in (pl.)! — Take a seat (formal)!

items.note: du-form is the bare stem (chum, gang, nimm, lueg); plural and Sie add -ed (chömed, nämed Si). 'Bitte' or 'schnell' softens a bare imperative.

items.target: ___, drum ___ / also ___

example.target: Es hät grägnet, drum bin ich dihei blibe.
example.gloss: It rained, so I stayed at home.

items.note: 'drum' (Standard 'darum/deshalb') in first position pushes the verb before the subject. 'also' at the start means 'so, well then'.

items.target: wo ___ (past, once) / wänn ___ (future, repeated)

example.target: Wo ich chli gsi bi, ha ich z Bärn gwohnt. Wänn ich Ziit ha, choche ich.
example.gloss: When I was little, I lived in Bern. When I have time, I cook.

items.note: Two words: 'wo' for a single past event (Standard 'als'), 'wänn' for future or repeated (Standard 'wenn'). Both verb-final.

items.target: bevor ___ / nach em ___ / nachdem ___

example.target: Bevor ich gang, rüef ich dir aa. Nach em Ässe gömmer go spaziere.
example.gloss: Before I go, I'll call you. After eating we'll go for a walk.

items.note: 'bevor' is verb-final; 'nachdem' exists but speech prefers 'nach em' plus noun or 'und dänn'. 'vorhär' and 'nachhär' are the adverbs.

items.target: wänn ___ (verb-final) / falls ___

example.target: Wänn du Ziit häsch, chum verbii.
example.gloss: If you have time, come by.

items.note: Same word as 'when': context decides. 'falls' (in case) is a bit more formal. Verb to the end, main clause then starts with its verb.

items.target: ___, dass ___ (verb-final)

example.target: Ich glaub, dass er rächt hät.
example.gloss: I think that he's right.

items.note: 'dass' sends the verb to the end. Dropping it is more common than in German: 'ich glaub, er hät rächt'.

items.target: ___, wo ___ (verb-final)

example.target: Das isch de Kolleg, wo i Bärn wohnt. Das isch s Buech, wo ich läse.
example.gloss: That's the mate who lives in Bern. That's the book that I'm reading.

items.note: One universal relative 'wo' for all genders and numbers, subject or object. Standard 'der/die/das' as relatives are never used in dialect.

items.target: sit ___ (dative; both for and since)

example.target: Ich wohne sit zwei Jahr i Züri, sit em Januar im Kreis 4.
example.gloss: I've lived in Zürich for two years, since January in District 4.

items.note: 'sit' (Standard 'seit') covers both: sit zwei Jahr (for), sit Mäntig (since). Verb in the present, not the Perfekt, because it still holds.

items.target: bis ___

example.target: Ich schaffe bis am Sächsi. Bis morn!
example.gloss: I work until six. See you tomorrow!

items.note: 'bis' plus a time takes 'am' (bis am Sächsi). As a conjunction it is verb-final: bis du chunsch. 'Bis dänn' means 'see you then'.

items.target: über ___ (accusative) / vo ___ (dative)

example.target: Mir händ über d Arbet gredt. Er hät vo sine Ferie verzellt.
example.gloss: We talked about work. He told us about his holidays.

items.note: 'rede über' takes accusative, 'verzelle vo' takes dative. 'Es gaat um' is 'it's about' for topics; 'ungefähr' is the other 'about'.

items.target: zerscht ___, dänn ___, nachhär ___, am Schluss ___

example.target: Zerscht simmer go poschte, dänn händ mir kochet, und am Schluss händ mir gässe.
example.gloss: First we went shopping, then we cooked, and finally we ate.

items.note: Each adverb takes first position and flips verb and subject (dänn händ mir). 'simmer' = sind mir, 'gömmer' = gönd mir.

items.target: min, din, sin, ire, üse, eue, ire / mini, dini (f./pl.), mis, dis (n.)

example.target: Min Brüeder, mini Schwöschter, mis Chind. Das isch üses Huus.
example.gloss: My brother, my sister, my child. That's our house.

items.note: Endings by gender: min (m.), mini (f. and pl.), mis (n.). 'üse' (our) and 'eue' (your pl.) differ from Standard unser/euer. Dative: mim, minere.

items.target: es paar, e chli, vil, wenig, en Huufe, nüt
items.gloss: a few, a bit, much/many, little, a lot, nothing

example.target: Ich ha e chli Ziit und es paar Fränkli. Es hät vil Lüüt, aber nüt z ässe.
example.gloss: I've a bit of time and a few francs. There are lots of people, but nothing to eat.

items.note: 'vil' covers much and many. 'e chli' is a bit; 'en Huufe' (a heap) is the casual 'a lot'. 'öppis' = something, 'nüt' = nothing, 'kei' = no/none.

items.target: adjective + -er als ___

example.target: Züri isch grösser als Bärn, aber Bärn isch schöner.
example.gloss: Zürich is bigger than Bern, but Bern is prettier.

items.note: 'als' after the comparative, as in Standard German (never 'wie'). Umlaut in short adjectives: gross/grösser, alt/elter, jung/jünger, guet/besser.

items.target: z ___ / gnueg / sehr, mega, uu

example.target: Das isch z tüür. Häsch gnueg Gäld? Es isch uu schön.
example.gloss: That's too expensive. Do you have enough money? It's really beautiful.

items.note: 'z' before an adjective is 'too' (z tüür = zu teuer). 'gnueg' goes before the noun. 'uu' and 'mega' are the spoken 'very'; 'sehr' sounds bookish.

items.target: dative: em / de / em, mir / dir / ihm / ire / üs / eu / ine

example.target: Ich gib em Peter s Buech. Chasch mer d Butter gää?
example.gloss: I give Peter the book. Can you pass me the butter?

items.note: Dative person before accusative thing, as in German. Articles: em (m./n.), de (f.), de (pl.). Pronoun order: 'gib mer s' = give it to me.

items.target: de Zug (train), s Billet (ticket), s GA (rail pass), s Halbtax (half-fare card), s Gleis (platform), d Aachunft (arrival), d Abfahrt (departure), umschtiige (change trains), s Velo (bike), s Auto (car), s Hotel (hotel), s Zimmer (room), reserviere (book), d Ferie (holidays), d Reis (trip), de Flughafe (airport)
items.note: 'Billet' (from French) is the ticket, 'Velo' the bike, 'Ferie' the holidays. Standard Fahrkarte, Fahrrad, Urlaub are never used.

items.target: poschte (to shop), de Lade (shop), d Migros / de Coop (supermarkets), d Chleider (clothes), d Hose (trousers), s Hemd (shirt), d Schue (shoes), d Jacke (jacket), d Grössi (size), aaprobiere (try on), tüür (expensive), günschtig (cheap), s Gäld (money), de Franke (franc), de Rappe (cent), d Kasse (till), zahle (pay), d Aktion (special offer)
items.note: 'poschte' (go shopping, from Post) is the everyday verb; 'iichaufe' is Standard-flavoured. 'billig' means cheap-and-nasty; say 'günschtig'.

items.target: de Arzt (doctor), d Ärztin (doctor f.), s Spital (hospital), d Apitheek (pharmacy), chrank (ill), gsund (healthy), d Verchältig (cold), s Fieber (fever), de Huesta (cough), d Chopfweh (headache), de Buuch (belly), de Rugge (back), s Bei (leg), d Hand (hand), s Medikamänt (medicine), weh tue (to hurt)
items.note: 'Ich ha Chopfweh' (I have a headache), 'es tuet mer weh' (it hurts). Doctor's talk: 'Wo tuets weh?' 'Sind Si krankgschribe?' (signed off sick).

items.target: d Arbet (work), schaffe (to work), s Büro (office), de Chef (boss), d Chefin (boss f.), de Kolleg (colleague), d Sitzig (meeting), s Projäkt (project), d Uni (university), s Studium (studies), d Prüefig (exam), lerne (learn/study), de Lohn (salary), d Kündigung (notice), Teilziit (part-time), d Stell (job/position)
items.note: 'schaffe' is to work, 'd Arbet' the work (Standard 'arbeiten/Arbeit'). 'Sitzig' is a meeting; 'Stell' a post. 'lerne' means both learn and study for.

items.target: s Wätter (weather), d Sunne (sun), de Räge (rain), rägne (to rain), de Schnee (snow), schneie (to snow), de Wind (wind), de Näbel (fog), chalt (cold), warm (warm), heiss (hot), schön (nice), de Früelig (spring), de Summer (summer), de Herbscht (autumn), de Winter (winter), d Bise (cold north-east wind), de Föhn (warm alpine wind)
items.note: 'Es rägnet' / 'es schneit'. The Bise and the Föhn are real weather words every Zürcher uses; Föhn also gives people headaches.

items.target: uufstaa (get up), zmörgele (have breakfast), dusche (shower), aalegge (get dressed), go schaffe (go to work), zmittage (have lunch), heicho (come home), choche (cook), abwäsche (wash up), putze (clean), wäsche (do laundry), iichaufe / poschte (shop), s Wohnzimmer (living room), d Chuchi (kitchen), s Bad (bathroom), s Schlafzimmer (bedroom), is Bett gaa (go to bed)
items.note: Meal verbs are one word: zmörgele, zmittage, znachte. 'heicho' is come home, 'dihei' at home. 'Chuchi' is the kitchen (hence Chuchichäschtli).

items.target: Stress on the new word; unstressed pronouns shrink (mer, der, em, si)
items.note: Stressed content words stand out, pronouns and articles almost vanish: 'Gisch mer s?' sounds like 'gischmers'. Practice the shrinking forms mer/der/em/ere.

items.target: Rising tune on yes/no questions; falling on wh-questions; the 'oder?' tag
items.note: Yes/no questions rise sharply at the end (Chunsch MIT?); wh-questions fall like statements. The tag 'oder?' at the end also rises and is very frequent.

items.target: Häsch Luscht, ___? / Wotsch ___? / Möchted Si ___?
items.gloss: Do you feel like ___? / Do you want ___? / Would you like ___?

example.target: Häsch Luscht, morn go wandere? — Wotsch en Kafi?
example.gloss: Do you feel like hiking tomorrow? — Want a coffee?

items.note: 'Häsch Luscht' (with du) is the invitation; 'wotsch' is direct but normal among friends. With Sie: 'Möchted Si' or 'Wänd Si'.

items.target: Merci, aber ___ / Das isch lieb, aber ___

example.target: Das isch lieb, aber ich cha leider nöd.
example.gloss: That's kind, but unfortunately I can't.

items.note: 'Das isch lieb' softens a refusal. Follow with 'leider' (unfortunately) and a 'wil' clause.

items.target: Wie wärs mit ___? / Was isch mit ___?

example.target: Wie wärs mit Samschtig? — Was isch mit Sunntig?
example.gloss: How about Saturday? — What about Sunday?

items.note: 'mit' takes the dative (mit em Samschtig, mit ere Pizza), but bare weekdays are fine. 'Wie wärs' = wie wär es.

items.target: Sorry, dass ich z spaat bi

example.target: Sorry, dass ich z spaat bi, s Tram isch nöd cho.
example.gloss: Sorry I'm late, the tram didn't come.

items.note: 'z spaat' (Standard 'zu spät') with 'dass' sending 'bi' to the end. Or simply 'Sorry, ich bi z spaat'.

items.target: Zahle, bitte / Chönd mer zahle?
items.gloss: The bill, please / Can we pay?

example.target: Zahle, bitte! — Zäme oder getrennt?
example.gloss: The bill, please! — Together or separately?

items.note: Swiss say 'zahle' (to pay), not 'die Rechnung'. Expect the question 'zäme oder getrennt' and answer 'zäme'.

items.target: Was heisst ___?

example.target: Was heisst 'Znüni'? — Es Znüni isch de Znüni... e chlini Mahlziit am Nüni.
example.gloss: What does 'Znüni' mean? — A Znüni is... a little meal at nine.

items.note: 'heisse' means 'mean' as well as 'be called'. 'Was heisst das uf Änglisch?' gets a translation.

items.target: Bis dänn! / Bis morn! / Bis spöter!
items.gloss: See you then / see you tomorrow / see you later

example.target: Also, bis morn am Achti! — Bis dänn, tschau!
example.gloss: Right, see you tomorrow at eight! — See you then, bye!

items.note: 'bis' plus any time word. 'Also' at the start signals the conversation is ending.

items.target: Tönt guet / Isch guet / Passt
items.gloss: Sounds good / OK, fine / Works for me

example.target: Sölled mer am Sibni? — Passt, tönt guet.
example.gloss: Shall we do seven? — Works for me, sounds good.

items.note: 'tönt' (Standard 'klingt') is the Swiss verb for sounds. 'Isch guet' and 'passt' also close a plan; 'abgmacht' = deal.

items.target: Ich finde, ___ / Was meinsch du?
items.gloss: I think ___ / What do you think?

example.target: Ich finde, Homeoffice isch super. Was meinsch du?
example.gloss: I think working from home is great. What do you think?

items.note: Uses C-IN-MY-OPINION, C-WHAT-DO-YOU-THINK, D-THINK-THAT. 'Ich finde' plus main-clause order is the everyday opinion; 'Minere Meinig nah' is for discussions.

items.target: Gnau, das gseh ich au so / Ja scho, aber ___
items.gloss: Exactly, I see it that way too / Yes, sure, but ___

example.target: Ja scho, aber ich gseh das e chli anders.
example.gloss: Yes, sure, but I see that a bit differently.

items.note: Uses C-I-AGREE, C-SEE-POINT-BUT, G-BUT. 'Ja scho, aber' is the Swiss partial agreement; 'Ich bi nöd iiverstande' is the direct disagreement.

items.target: ___, wil ___ / Zum Bispil ___

example.target: Ich fahre lieber mit em Zug, wil s entspannter isch. Zum Bispil cha ich läse.
example.gloss: I prefer the train, because it's more relaxed. For example, I can read.

items.note: Uses G-BECAUSE, G-SINCE-AS, G-ALSO. 'wil' verb-final; 'zum Bispil' (z.B.) in first position flips verb and subject.

items.target: Wo ich ___, isch ___ / Uf eimal ___ / Dänn ___

example.target: Wo ich am Bahnhof aacho bi, isch de Zug grad abgfahre. Also bin ich go Kafi trinke.
example.gloss: When I arrived at the station, the train had just left. So I went for a coffee.

items.note: Recipe: G-WHEN (wo), D-HAD-DONE, G-SO, G-SEQUENCE. Everything in the Perfekt; 'grad' and 'scho' replace the missing past perfect.

items.target: Sorry, aber ___ gaat nöd / Chönted Si ___?
items.gloss: Sorry, but ___ doesn't work / Could you ___?

example.target: Sorry, aber s WLAN gaat nöd und s Zimmer isch mega luut. Chönted Si mer es anders gää?
example.gloss: Sorry, but the wifi doesn't work and the room is really loud. Could you give me another?

items.note: Uses C-THE-THING-IS, D-COULD, G-AND. Swiss complain softly: start with 'Sorry, aber' or 'Es isch so', then 'chönted Si' for the request.

items.target: Wie wärs mit ___? / Das gaat leider nöd / Dänn mache mers so
items.gloss: How about ___? / That doesn't work / Then let's do it that way

example.target: Wie wärs mit Samschtig? — Das gaat leider nöd. Sunntig? — Guet, dänn mache mers so.
example.gloss: How about Saturday? — That doesn't work, sorry. Sunday? — Good, then we'll do it that way.

items.note: Uses C-HOW-ABOUT, D-WOULD-RATHER, C-SOUNDS-GOOD. 'mache mers' = mache mir es. 'Abgmacht' closes the deal.

items.target: Du söttsch ___ / A dinere Stell würd ich ___ / Pass uf, ___
items.gloss: You should ___ / In your place I would ___ / Watch out, ___

example.target: Du söttsch früener aafange z lerne. A dinere Stell würd ich de Lehrer frage.
example.gloss: You should start studying earlier. In your place I'd ask the teacher.

items.note: Uses D-SHOULD, C-IF-I-WERE-YOU, D-SHOULD-HAVE. 'Pass uf' (watch out) and 'du muesch unbedingt' are the warning forms.

items.target: Er hät gseit, dass ___ / Si hät gseit, ich söll ___
items.gloss: He said that ___ / She asked if ___ / She said I should ___

example.target: D Chefin hät gseit, d Deadline isch jetzt Donschtig, und ich söll s Team informiere.
example.gloss: The boss said the deadline is now Thursday, and I should inform the team.

items.note: Uses D-SAID-THAT, D-TOLD-TO, G-THAT. No subjunctive shift: keep the original tense after 'dass'. Requests are reported with 'söll'.

items.target: ich ha scho ___, wo ___ / ich ha ___ gha, wo ___

example.target: Ich ha scho gässe gha, wo si cho isch.
example.gloss: I had already eaten when she came.

items.note: Dialect has no Plusquamperfekt; the doubled Perfekt (ha ... gha / bi ... gsi) is the substitute, and 'scho' alone often suffices. 'wo' = when (past).

items.target: ich ___ sit ___ (present)

example.target: Ich lerne sit drei Monet Schwiizerdütsch.
example.gloss: I've been learning Swiss German for three months.

items.note: Present tense plus 'sit' (for/since) as in Standard German. Never Perfekt: 'ich ha glernt sit' means it has stopped.

items.target: er mues ___ sii / das cha nöd ___ sii / er isch sicher ___
items.gloss: he must be ___ / that can't be ___ / he's surely ___

example.target: Er isch sicher chrank. Das cha nöd stimme.
example.gloss: He must be ill. That can't be right.

items.note: Deduction is usually 'sicher' (surely) or 'wahrschiinlich' plus the plain verb; 'mues ... sii' works but 'sicher' is more natural. Negative: 'cha nöd'.

items.target: ich hett ___ sölle

example.target: Ich hett früener aafange sölle.
example.gloss: I should have started earlier.

items.note: 'hett' plus infinitive plus bare 'sölle' at the very end (Standard 'hätte ... sollen'). The most useful regret door.

items.target: ich hett ___ chöne

example.target: Er hett au aalüüte chöne.
example.gloss: He could have called too.

items.note: Same shape as D-SHOULD-HAVE with 'chöne'. Past ability without regret is Perfekt: 'ich ha nöd cho chöne'.

items.target: ich würd lieber ___ / ich gang lieber ___

example.target: Ich würd lieber i d Bärge gaa als as Meer.
example.gloss: I'd rather go to the mountains than to the seaside.

items.note: 'lieber' after the verb; 'würd' plus infinitive is the conditional. 'Mir wärs lieber, wänn' for a full clause preference.

items.target: Wänn ich ___ wär, würd ich ___

example.target: Wänn ich riich wär, würd ich weniger schaffe.
example.gloss: If I were rich, I'd work less.

items.note: 'wär' (Standard 'wäre'), 'hett' (hätte), 'chönnt' (könnte) are the short conditionals; everything else uses 'würd' plus infinitive. Both halves may take 'würd' in speech.

items.target: ich wett, ich hett ___ / ich wett, ich chönnt ___
items.gloss: I wish I had ___ / I wish I could ___

example.target: Ich wett, ich hett meh Ziit. Ich wett, ich chönnt fliege.
example.gloss: I wish I had more time. I wish I could fly.

items.note: 'ich wett' (wetti) is 'I'd want' and introduces a conditional clause without 'dass'. Standard 'ich wünschte' is never said.

items.target: si hät gseit, ich söll ___ / si hät mich gfragt, öb ich ___
items.gloss: she told me to ___ / she asked me to ___

example.target: Si hät gseit, ich söll s Team informiere.
example.gloss: She told me to inform the team.

items.note: Commands are reported with 'söll' in a dass-less clause; polite requests with 'gfragt, öb ich ... chönnt'. No 'zu' infinitive as in Standard 'bat mich zu'.

items.target: er hät gseit, (dass) ___ / er hät gfragt, öb ___

example.target: Er hät gseit, dass er morn chunt. Si hät gfragt, öb ich Ziit ha.
example.gloss: He said that he's coming tomorrow. She asked if I have time.

items.note: No subjunctive I (Standard 'er komme'): report in the original tense. Dialect reportive 'er chömi/er heigi' exists in Zürich but is optional. 'öb' = whether.

items.target: Chönd Si mer säge, wo ___? / Weisch, wänn ___?
items.gloss: Could you tell me where ___? / Do you know when ___?

example.target: Chönd Si mer säge, wo de Zug uf Bärn abfahrt?
example.gloss: Could you tell me where the train to Bern leaves from?

items.note: Indirect question: verb goes to the end (abfahrt). 'Weisch' (do you know) is the du version. For yes/no use 'öb'.

items.target: es isch ___ worde / es isch us ___ / me hät ___
items.gloss: it was ___ / it is made of ___ / they ___

example.target: S Huus isch 1900 baut worde. De Tisch isch us Holz. Me hät s renoviert.
example.gloss: The house was built in 1900. The table is of wood. It was renovated.

items.note: Passive exists (wärde plus participle, past 'isch ... worde') but speech prefers 'me' (one, Standard 'man'). Material: 'us' plus noun, no participle.

items.target: ich bi s gwöhnt, ___ z ___ / ich gwöhne mich a ___
items.gloss: I'm used to ___-ing / I'm getting used to ___

example.target: Ich bi s gwöhnt, früeh uufzstaa. Ich gwöhne mich langsam a s Wätter.
example.gloss: I'm used to getting up early. I'm slowly getting used to the weather.

items.note: 's gwöhnt sii' plus 'z' infinitive; 'sich gwöhne a' plus accusative. Standard 'gewöhnt' loses its vowel: gwöhnt.

items.target: si hät mich ___ laa / si hät mich zwunge, ___ z ___
items.gloss: she let me ___ / she made me ___

example.target: Si hät mich gaa laa, aber er hät mich zwunge z warte.
example.gloss: She let me go, but he made me wait.

items.note: 'laa' (lassen) uses a bare infinitive in the Perfekt: hät ... laa, no participle. 'made me' is 'zwunge' (forced) or 'ich ha müese'.

items.target: ich sött eigentli ___ / du gaasch besser ___

example.target: Ich sött eigentli lerne. Du gaasch besser jetzt.
example.gloss: I'm supposed to be studying. You'd better go now.

items.note: 'sött eigentli' (should actually) is the 'supposed to' of the dialect. 'you'd better' is imperative or 'gaasch besser' with 'besser' after the verb.

items.target: ich wird ___ chöne / ich ha ___ chöne
items.gloss: I'll be able to ___ / I was able to ___

example.target: Ich wird morn nöd cho chöne. Geschter ha ich alles mache chöne.
example.gloss: I won't be able to come tomorrow. Yesterday I could do everything.

items.note: Both turns keep 'chöne' as a bare infinitive at the end (never a participle 'gchönt'). Future 'wird' is optional: 'morn cha ich nöd'.

items.target: ha/bi + participle + gha/gsi

example.target: Wo ich cho bi, hät er scho gässe gha.
example.gloss: When I came, he had already eaten.

items.note: The doubled Perfekt is the only past-before-past and is used mainly to make sequence explicit. Plain Perfekt plus 'scho' or 'vorhär' is the usual choice.

items.target: present + sit / scho ___ lang

example.target: Ich warte scho e Stund. Ich schaffe sit 2020 daa.
example.gloss: I've been waiting for an hour. I've been working here since 2020.

items.note: No such tense: present with 'sit' (since/for) or 'scho' plus duration. Perfekt would mean the action is over.

items.target: wird + participle / isch + participle + worde

example.target: D Strass wird repariert. De Lade isch gschlosse worde.
example.gloss: The road is being repaired. The shop was closed.

items.note: Formed like Standard German ('worde' for 'worden'), but speech reaches for 'me' first: me repariert d Strass. State passive: isch gschlosse.

items.target: wänn ___ wär/hett/würd ___, (dänn) würd ___

example.target: Wänn ich meh Ziit hett, würd ich meh reise.
example.gloss: If I had more time, I'd travel more.

items.note: Short conditionals for sii, haa, modals (wär, hett, chönnt, müesst, wett, sött); 'würd' plus infinitive for all other verbs, in both halves if needed.

items.target: hät gseit, dass + original tense / söll for orders

example.target: Er hät gseit, dass er chrank isch und dass ich warte söll.
example.gloss: He said he's ill and that I should wait.

items.note: There is no tense shift and no Konjunktiv I: keep the speaker's tense. Zürich has an optional reportive (er sägi, er heigi) that you will hear but need not use.

items.target: obwohl ___ (verb-final) / au wänn ___

example.target: Obwohl s rägnet, gang ich go laufe.
example.gloss: Although it's raining, I'm going for a walk.

items.note: 'obwohl' verb-final, then the main clause starts with its verb. 'au wänn' (even if/though) is the more spoken alternative.

items.target: während ___ (verb-final) / ___, dagäge ___

example.target: Während ich choche, chasch du de Tisch decke. Züri isch tüür, Bärn dagäge günschtiger.
example.gloss: While I cook, you can set the table. Zürich is expensive, Bern by contrast cheaper.

items.note: Temporal 'während' is verb-final. For contrast, dialect prefers two main clauses with 'dagäge' or 'aber' rather than 'während'.

items.target: wil ___ / da ___ (verb-final)

example.target: Da ich sowieso i de Stadt bi, chum ich schnell verbii.
example.gloss: Since I'm in town anyway, I'll drop by quickly.

items.note: 'wil' is the all-purpose reason word; 'da' is a bit formal and puts the reason first. 'sit' is never a reason word, only time.

items.target: damit ___ (verb-final)

example.target: Ich schriib s uf, damit ich s nöd vergisse.
example.gloss: I'm writing it down so that I don't forget it.

items.note: 'damit' with a full clause, verb at the end. Where subjects match, 'zum' plus infinitive (G-IN-ORDER-TO) is more natural.

items.target: zum ___ / für z ___ / um ___ z ___

example.target: Ich gang i d Stadt zum poschte. Ich bruuche Ziit für z lerne.
example.gloss: I'm going into town to shop. I need time to study.

items.note: 'zum' plus bare infinitive is pure dialect (Standard 'um ... zu'). 'für z' is also common. 'um ... z' sounds like Standard German.

items.target: wo ___ (place, time) / wo ___ sin/ire ___ (whose)

example.target: Das isch s Kafi, wo mir üs kenneglernt händ. Das isch de Maa, wo sis Auto kaputt isch.
example.gloss: That's the café where we met. That's the man whose car is broken.

items.note: Still 'wo' for everything, including place and time. 'Whose' is 'wo' plus a possessive (wo sin, wo iri); there is no 'dessen/deren'.

items.target: warte uf, dänke a, abhänge vo, sich interessiere für, sich freue uf
items.gloss: wait for, think of, depend on, be interested in, look forward to

example.target: Ich warte uf de Bus. Ich freu mich uf d Ferie. Es hängt vom Wätter ab.
example.gloss: I'm waiting for the bus. I'm looking forward to the holidays. It depends on the weather.

items.note: Also: rede über, sich ärgere über, fröge nach, hälfe bi, achte uf. uf/über take accusative, vo/bi/nach dative; da-forms are druf, dra, davo, defür.

items.target: entweder ___ oder ___ / weder ___ no ___ / ich au nöd
items.gloss: either ... or / neither ... nor / me neither

example.target: Entweder chunsch jetzt oder gar nöd. Ich mag weder Kafi no Tee. — Ich au nöd.
example.gloss: Either you come now or not at all. I like neither coffee nor tea. — Me neither.

items.note: 'weder ... no' (Standard 'weder ... noch'). 'Me neither' is 'ich au nöd'; 'me too' is 'ich au'.

items.target: sobald ___ (verb-final) / bis ___
items.gloss: as soon as / by the time

example.target: Sobald ich fertig bi, rüef ich aa. Bis du chunsch, han ich kochet.
example.gloss: As soon as I'm done, I'll call. By the time you come, I'll have cooked.

items.note: 'sobald' verb-final, main clause in the present. 'By the time' is 'bis' plus clause, with Perfekt for the completed action.

items.target: statt ___ / anstatt z ___ / usser ___

example.target: Statt Bier nimm ich en Wii. Usser em Peter chömed alli.
example.gloss: Instead of beer I'll take a wine. Apart from Peter everyone is coming.

items.note: 'statt' plus noun or 'anstatt z' plus infinitive. 'usser' (Standard 'außer') takes the dative: usser em Peter, usser mir.

items.target: wo (all roles); dative: wo ... em/ere; preposition: wo ... drin/dra

example.target: De Maa, wo ich gseh ha. D Frau, wo ich ere ghulfe ha. S Huus, wo ich drin wohne.
example.gloss: The man I saw. The woman I helped. The house I live in.

items.note: 'wo' never changes; a role other than subject/object is shown by a resumptive pronoun inside the clause (wo ich ere ghulfe ha) or a da-form (wo ich drin wohne).

items.target: mich, dich, sich, üs, eu, sich (mir, dir dative)

example.target: Ich freu mich uf d Ferie. Mir träffed üs am Sächsi. Ich wäsch mer d Händ.
example.gloss: I'm looking forward to the holidays. We're meeting at six. I'm washing my hands.

items.note: Same set as Standard German except 'üs' and 'eu'. Common reflexives: sich freue, sich träffe, sich erinnere, sich beeile (hurry), sich uufrege.

items.target: e chli, es bitzeli, zimli, rächt, chuum, gar nöd
items.gloss: a bit, a tiny bit, quite, rather, hardly, not at all

example.target: Es isch zimli chalt und ich ha chuum gschlafe. Ich bi es bitzeli müed.
example.gloss: It's quite cold and I hardly slept. I'm a tiny bit tired.

items.note: 'e chli' and 'es bitzeli' are the softeners you will hear constantly. 'zimli' = quite/pretty, 'chuum' = hardly, 'gar nöd' = not at all.

items.target: de/d/s ___-scht / am ___-schte / so ___ wie

example.target: Das isch de schönscht Platz i Züri. Er lauft am schnällschte. Si isch so gross wie ich.
example.gloss: That's the nicest place in Zürich. He runs fastest. She's as tall as me.

items.note: Superlative -scht (Standard -st) with umlaut: grösscht, elscht, bescht. 'so ... wie' for equality, 'als' only for comparatives.

items.target: not applicable: no genitive; vo + dative / dative + possessive

example.target: S Auto vo mim Brüeder. Em Peter sis Auto. D Tür vom Huus.
example.gloss: My brother's car. Peter's car. The door of the house.

items.note: There is no genitive at all in dialect. Use 'vo' (vom, vo de) or the dative-possessive: em Peter sis (Peter's), de Anna ires (Anna's). 'Peters Auto' sounds foreign.

items.target: d Meinig (opinion), meine (to think/mean), finde (to find/think), s Argumänt (argument), de Grund (reason), s Bispil (example), d Ziitig (newspaper), d Nachrichte (news), s Fernseh (TV), s Radio (radio), s SRF (Swiss broadcaster), diskutiere (discuss), rächt haa (be right), iiverstande (agreed), dagäge (against), defür (for)
items.note: 'meine' is 'think' in the sense of opinion; 'dänke' is more 'think, reflect'. 'Ich bi iiverstande' = I agree. 'Ziitig' is the newspaper.

items.target: froh (glad), truurig (sad), hässig (angry), nervös (nervous), müed (tired), gschtresst (stressed), sich freue (be glad), Angscht haa (be afraid), lieb haa (love), gern haa (like), de Fründ / d Fründin (partner), d Beziehig (relationship), verliebt (in love), s Vertraue (trust), sich striite (argue), sich versöhne (make up)
items.note: 'hässig' means angry, not hateful (a false friend with Standard 'hässlich'). 'Ich ha dich gern' says love to family and friends; 'ich liebe dich' is heavy.

items.target: d Umwält (environment), d Natur (nature), de Wald (forest), de Bärg (mountain), d Bärge (mountains), de See (lake), de Fluss (river), d Luft (air), s Klima (climate), de Abfall (rubbish), rezyklere (recycle), de Verkehr (traffic), s Quartier (neighbourhood), d Stadt (city), s Dorf (village), ufem Land (in the countryside)
items.note: 'Quartier' (from French) is the neighbourhood, 'Kreis' the numbered Zürich district. Recycling talk: 'de Güsel' is Zürich slang for rubbish, 'de Kehricht' the standard word.

items.target: d Schuel (school), d Lehr (apprenticeship), d Matura (school-leaving exam), d Uni / d ETH (university), s Studium (studies), studiere (study at uni), lerne (learn/study), d Prüefig (exam), bestah (pass), duregheie (fail), de Kurs (course), d Uusbildig (training), de Abschluss (degree), d Karriere (career), s Praktikum (internship), bewärbe (apply)
items.note: Two thirds of Swiss do a 'Lehr' (apprenticeship), so it comes up constantly. 'duregheie' (fall through) is the spoken 'fail an exam'. 'lerne' = study for, 'studiere' = be at university.

items.target: d Wohnig (flat), s Huus (house), miete (rent), d Miete (rent money), de Vermieter (landlord), d Verwaltig (property management), de Nachbar (neighbour), d Nachbere (neighbour f.), s Zimmer (room), d Chuchi (kitchen), s Bad (bathroom), de Balkon (balcony), d Wäschchuchi (laundry room), d Nebechöschte (service charges), kündige (give notice), umzieh / züügle (move house), d Waschig-Plan (laundry rota)
items.note: 'züügle' is the pure dialect word for moving house. The 'Waschchuchi' rota and 'Nachtruhe' after 22:00 are the classic neighbour flashpoints.

items.target: s Handy / s Natel (mobile), de Compi (computer), s Internet (internet), s WLAN (wifi), d Website (website), d App (app), s Passwort (password), abelade (download), ufelade (upload), s Mail (email), schriibe (text/write), aalüüte (call), d Nachricht (message), s Foti (photo), de Bildschirm (screen), lade (charge), d Verbindig (connection)
items.note: 'Natel' is the old Swiss word for mobile, 'Handy' is winning. 'aalüüte' (ring up) is the phone verb, 'Compi' the computer, 's Foti' a photo.

items.target: Clitics: gömmer, hämmer, simmer, gisch mers, isches; final -n mostly gone
items.note: Verb plus 'mir' fuses: gömmer (gönd mir), hämmer (händ mir), simmer (sind mir), müemmer. Pronoun chains shrink: 'gisch mers' (give me it), 'häschs' (have you it).

items.target: Unstressed 'e' and 'ich' shrink; 'i' for ich; 'ned/nöd/nid' variants; Bern/Basel vowel shifts
items.gloss: Following native speed: what gets swallowed
items.note: Fast speech drops 'ich' to 'i' (i gang, i weiss) and 'es' to 's' (s isch, s gaat). Expect nöd/nid/nit/ned for 'not' across the Swiss regions; Bern has 'ig' for 'ich' and 'nid'.

items.target: Ich finde, ___ / Minere Meinig nah ___ / Ich glaub, ___
items.gloss: I think ___ / In my opinion ___ / I believe ___

example.target: Ich finde, das isch e gueti Idee. Minere Meinig nah bruuchts meh Ziit.
example.gloss: I think that's a good idea. In my opinion it needs more time.

items.note: 'Ich finde' is the everyday opinion opener; 'Minere Meinig nah' (dative plus 'nah') is for discussions and flips verb and subject.

items.target: Gnau / Das stimmt / Du häsch rächt

example.target: Gnau, das gseh ich au so. Du häsch rächt.
example.gloss: Exactly, I see it the same way. You're right.

items.note: 'Gnau' (Standard 'genau') is the reflex of agreement. 'Ich bi iiverstande' is 'I agree' when a decision is at stake.

items.target: Ich verstaa dich scho, aber ___ / Ja scho, aber ___
items.gloss: I see your point, but ___ / Yes, sure, but ___

example.target: Ich verstaa dich scho, aber das isch mer z tüür.
example.gloss: I see your point, but that's too expensive for me.

items.note: 'scho' (already/indeed) marks the concession. 'Ja scho, aber' is shorter and very Swiss.

items.target: S Problem isch, ___ / Es isch so: ___
items.gloss: The thing is, ___ / It's like this: ___

example.target: S Problem isch, ich ha am Friitig e Sitzig.
example.gloss: The thing is, I have a meeting on Friday.

items.note: 'S Problem isch' followed by a main clause (no 'dass' needed). 'Es isch so' (it's like this) prefaces bad news or a complaint.

items.target: Was meinsch? / Was meined Si? / Wie gsehsch du das?
items.gloss: What do you think? / What do you think (formal)? / How do you see it?

example.target: Ich finde s z tüür. Was meinsch du?
example.gloss: I think it's too expensive. What do you think?

items.note: 'meine' is the verb for opinions; 'Was dänksch?' asks what is on your mind. 'Wie gsehsch du das?' invites a view.

items.target: A dinere Stell würd ich ___ / Ich würd ___
items.gloss: In your place I'd ___ / I would ___

example.target: A dinere Stell würd ich de Job nää.
example.gloss: If I were you I'd take the job.

items.note: 'A dinere Stell' (at your place, dative) is the Swiss shape; 'wänn ich du wär' is understood but rarer. Infinitive at the end.

items.target: Ehrlich gseit, ___ / Ganz ehrlich, ___

example.target: Ehrlich gseit, ich ha kei Luscht.
example.gloss: To be honest, I don't feel like it.

items.note: 'gseit' is the participle of 'säge' (Standard 'gesagt'). Comma, then a normal main clause; the phrase does not count as first position.

items.target: Chunt druf aa / Es chunt uf ___ aa

example.target: Chunsch morn? — Chunt druf aa, wie s Wätter isch.
example.gloss: Coming tomorrow? — Depends how the weather is.

items.note: 'aacho uf' (Standard 'ankommen auf'): 'es chunt druf aa' with the pronoun 'druf' (darauf). Follow with 'wie', 'öb' or 'uf' plus noun.

items.target: Erschtens ___, zweitens ___ / Es gaat drum, dass ___
items.gloss: Firstly ___, secondly ___ / The point is that ___

example.target: Erschtens spart me Ziit, zweitens isch me produktiver. Drum bin ich klar defür.
example.gloss: Firstly you save time, secondly you're more productive. So I'm clearly in favour.

items.note: Uses G-OTHER-HAND, C-ADMITTEDLY, G-HOWEVER. 'me' (one) carries general claims. Dialect argument sounds less formal than written German: short main clauses, 'drum', 'aber'.

items.target: Ich glaub, ___ / wahrschiinlich / e chli / villicht
items.gloss: I think ___ / probably / a bit / maybe

example.target: Ich glaub, das isch villicht e chli z optimistisch, aber ich bi mer nöd sicher.
example.gloss: I think that's maybe a bit too optimistic, but I'm not sure.

items.note: Uses D-THINK-THAT, D-MIGHT, S-QUANT-ADV. Stack 'ich glaub', 'villicht', 'e chli' and end with 'oder?' to soften; 'ich bi mer nöd sicher' takes the reflexive 'mer'.

items.target: Klar, ___, aber ___ / Das stimmt scho, trotzdem ___

example.target: Klar, s choscht meh, aber uf d Dauer lohnt sichs. Trotzdem find ichs riskant.
example.gloss: Sure, it costs more, but in the long run it pays off. I still find it risky.

items.note: Uses C-ADMITTEDLY, G-HOWEVER, C-THAT-SAID. 'scho' and 'klar' concede, 'trotzdem' in first position (verb next) counters.

items.target: Das chunt guet / Mach der kei Sorge / Glaub mer, ___
items.gloss: It'll be fine / Don't worry / Trust me, ___

example.target: Mach der kei Sorge, das chunt scho guet. Glaub mer, s lohnt sich.
example.gloss: Don't worry, it'll be fine. Trust me, it's worth it.

items.note: Uses T-IMPERATIVE, D-WILL, D-IF-I-WERE. 'Das chunt guet' (that comes good) is the all-purpose Swiss reassurance; 'scho' adds 'it will, you'll see'.

items.target: Uf de eine Siite ___, uf de andere ___ / Unter em Strich ___
items.gloss: On the one hand ___, on the other ___ / All in all ___

example.target: Einersiits isch d Stadt ruhiger, anderersiits lided d Läde. Unter em Strich bin ich defür.
example.gloss: On one hand the city is quieter, on the other the shops suffer. All in all I'm for it.

items.note: Uses G-OTHER-HAND, G-WHEREAS, C-ON-BALANCE. Each frame takes first position, so the verb comes right after it (isch, lided, bin).

items.target: Er isch wahrschiinlich ___ / Villicht hät er ___

example.target: Er hät wahrschiinlich de Zug verpasst, oder villicht isch er chrank worde.
example.gloss: He probably missed the train, or maybe he got ill.

items.note: Uses D-MUST-HAVE, D-COULD-HAVE, G-OR. The adverbs 'wahrschiinlich', 'sicher', 'villicht', 'wohl' plus the Perfekt do most speculation; modal-plus-infinitive is rarer than in English.

items.target: Ich hett ___ sölle / Wänn ich das gwüsst hett, hett ich ___
items.gloss: I should have ___ / If I'd known that, I'd have ___

example.target: Wänn ich das gwüsst hett, hett ich de Job gno. Schad, dass ich nöd gfragt ha.
example.gloss: If I'd known that, I'd have taken the job. A pity I didn't ask.

items.note: Uses D-IF-HAD-KNOWN, D-WISH-HAD, D-SHOULD-HAVE. All past hypotheticals use 'hett/wär' plus participle; 'schad' (shame/pity) plus 'dass' is the everyday regret.

items.target: Sehr geehrte ___ / Ich bitte Sie, ___ bis ___ zu ___
items.gloss: Dear ___ / I ask you to ___ by ___

example.target: Sehr geehrte Frau Meier, bitte lassen Sie die Heizung bis Freitag reparieren.
example.gloss: Dear Ms Meier, please have the heating repaired by Friday.

items.note: Formal writing is never in dialect: switch to Swiss Standard German (ss for ß, 'Freundliche Grüsse'). Recipe: C-I-WONDER-IF, D-HAVE-IT-DONE, G-AS-LONG-AS, all in Standard forms.

items.target: Wänn ich das gwüsst hett, hett ich ___ / wär ich ___
items.gloss: If I had known, I would have ___

example.target: Wänn ich das gwüsst hett, wär ich früener cho.
example.gloss: If I'd known, I'd have come earlier.

items.note: Third conditional: 'hett/wär' plus participle in both halves ('hätte gewusst, wäre gekommen'). Standard 'hätte ich ... gehabt' doubling is not needed.

items.target: si hät sicher ___ / si mues ___ haa / das cha nöd ___ sii
items.gloss: she must have ___ / she can't have ___

example.target: Si hät sicher de Zug verpasst. Si cha das nöd vergässe haa.
example.gloss: She must have missed the train. She can't have forgotten that.

items.note: Past deduction is usually 'sicher' or 'bestimmt' plus Perfekt. The modal shape 'mues ... haa' with participle exists but is heavier; 'cha nöd ... haa' for the negative.

items.target: bis ___ han ich ___ (Perfekt) / bis dänn isch ___ fertig
items.gloss: by ___ I'll have ___ / by then ___ will be done

example.target: Bis am Friitig han ich de Bricht fertig gschribe.
example.gloss: By Friday I'll have finished writing the report.

items.note: No future perfect: 'bis' plus time and the ordinary Perfekt read as future. 'ich wird ... gschribe haa' is possible but sounds translated.

items.target: dänn bin ich (am) ___ / i eme Jahr ___ ich ___
items.gloss: then I'll be ___-ing / in a year I'll ___

example.target: Nächscht Jahr um die Ziit bin ich wahrschiinlich am Studiere.
example.gloss: This time next year I'll probably be studying.

items.note: Present with a time frame; add 'am' plus infinitive if the ongoing sense matters. 'wird' would turn it into a guess about someone else.

items.target: ich ha scho ___ lang ___ gha, wo ___ / vorhär ha ich sit ___

example.target: Ich ha scho zwei Stund gwartet gha, wo si ändlich cho isch.
example.gloss: I'd been waiting two hours when she finally came.

items.note: Doubled Perfekt with 'scho' plus duration is the closest form; many speakers just say 'ich ha scho zwei Stund gwartet, wo ...'.

items.target: ich ha ___ ___ laa / ich laa ___ ___
items.gloss: I had ___ done / I'm having ___ done

example.target: Ich ha s Auto repariere laa. Ich laa mer d Haar schniide.
example.gloss: I had the car repaired. I'm having my hair cut.

items.note: 'laa' (lassen) plus bare infinitive; in the Perfekt 'laa' stays an infinitive at the end (repariere laa, not 'glaa'). Dative 'mer' for body parts.

items.target: ich wett, ich hett ___ / wänn ich nu ___ hett
items.gloss: I wish I had ___ / if only I had ___

example.target: Ich wett, ich hett früener aagfange. Wänn ich nu meh Ziit gha hett!
example.gloss: I wish I'd started earlier. If only I'd had more time!

items.note: 'ich wett' introduces the wish; the past wish takes 'hett/wär' plus participle. 'nu' (only) marks 'if only'.

items.target: früener sind mir immer ___ / als Chind hämmer jede ___
items.gloss: when I was young we would always ___

example.target: Früener simmer jede Summer i d Bärge ggange.
example.gloss: When I was young we'd go to the mountains every summer.

items.note: No 'would' habit form: 'früener' or 'als Chind' plus Perfekt plus 'immer' / 'jede'. Same as D-USED-TO.

items.target: er hät zuegää, dass ___ / er hät vorgschlage, ___ z ___

example.target: Er hät zuegää, dass er z spaat gsi isch, und hät vorgschlage, morn früener aazfange.
example.gloss: He admitted being late and suggested starting earlier tomorrow.

items.note: No -ing complements: 'dass' clause after zuegää, bestritte, or 'z' infinitive after vorschlaa. Note 'aazfange' (aa-z-fange): 'z' slips inside separable verbs.

items.target: si hät mer grate, ___ z ___ / si hät mich gwarnt, nöd ___ z ___
items.gloss: she advised me to ___ / she warned me not to ___

example.target: Si hät mer grate, früeh z buechet. Er hät mich gwarnt, nöd im Winter z fahre.
example.gloss: She advised me to book early. He warned me not to drive in winter.

items.note: 'rate' takes dative (mer), 'warne' accusative (mich), both with 'z' plus infinitive at the end. Standard 'geraten' shortens to 'grate'.

items.target: me seit, dass ___ / er söll aageblich ___ / es heisst, ___
items.gloss: they say that ___ / he's said to ___ / it's said ___

example.target: Me seit, dass er uuswanderet. Er söll aageblich mega riich sii.
example.gloss: They say he's emigrating. He's said to be very rich.

items.note: No impersonal passive 'es wird gesagt' in speech: use 'me seit' (one says) or 'es heisst'. 'söll' plus infinitive reports hearsay, as in Standard German.

items.target: Was ich wott, isch ___ / Es isch de/d ___, wo ___
items.gloss: What I want is ___ / It's ___ who/that ___

example.target: Was ich wott, isch meh Ziit. Es isch de Peter gsi, wo aaglüütet hät.
example.gloss: What I want is more time. It was Peter who called.

items.note: Cleft works with 'was ... isch' and 'es isch ... wo' ('wo' as universal relative). Fronting is more common than clefting: 'De Peter hät aaglüütet, nöd d Anna'.

items.target: Nöd nu ___, sondern au ___ / (no inversion: use two clauses)

example.target: Ich ha nöd nu de Bricht gschribe, ich ha au no d Sitzig vorbereitet.
example.gloss: Not only did I write the report, I also prepared the meeting.

items.note: English negative inversion has no dialect form; 'nöd nu ... sondern au' inside normal order carries it. Emphasis comes from fronting and 'au no' (on top).

items.target: du hettsch nöd ___ müese / ich ha nöd ___ müese
items.gloss: you needn't have ___ / I didn't need to ___

example.target: Du hettsch nöd cho müese! Ich ha zum Glück nöd warte müese.
example.gloss: You needn't have come! Luckily I didn't have to wait.

items.note: 'hettsch nöd ... müese' for the unnecessary act that happened; 'ha nöd ... müese' for the one that didn't. Bare infinitive 'müese' at the end, no participle.

items.target: bis + time + Perfekt

example.target: Bis am Sunntig han ich alles packt.
example.gloss: By Sunday I'll have packed everything.

items.note: Does not exist as a tense. 'bis' plus the Perfekt is understood as future-completed; 'wird ... haa' is Standard-German-flavoured.

items.target: present (+ am + infinitive) + time frame

example.target: Morn um die Ziit bin ich im Zug. Wahrschiinli bin ich grad am Schlaafe.
